claim: Kronander and Billard show that arbitrary time variation of impedance gains invalidates the standard fixed-gain energy argument: with constant virtual inertia, the classical storage derivative contains 0.5 q̃ᵀK̇q̃, so increasing stiffness can inject potential energy and produce instability even in free-space regulation. They derive a state-independent, offline-checkable sufficient condition coupling damping, stiffness, and both gain derivatives. Under exact dynamic decoupling and zero external torque, this condition guarantees global uniform stability, and strict inequalities give asymptotic stability. Simulations and offline checks of previously generated robot impedance profiles illustrate utility and conservatism, but the result is neither necessary nor a general passivity/contact-safety guarantee.
claim_locator: Section IV.B, validation of real impedance profiles
epistemic_status: qualified: the stability condition is theorem-supported and sufficient under explicit assumptions; comparative behavior is author-reported simulation and offline profile validation, not a general experimental proof of interaction passivity or robustness
problem_and_setting: The paper addresses execution of an already specified time-varying stiffness and damping profile in an impedance-controlled rigid manipulator. Fixed-gain impedance is passive with passive environments, but arbitrary gain variation can destroy that property. The aim is to determine before execution whether a desired profile is stable, rather than to learn the profile or adapt gains online.
method_or_mechanism: For closed-loop error dynamics Hq̃̈+D(t)q̃̇+K(t)q̃=τ_e with constant symmetric positive-definite H and symmetric positive-definite differentiable D(t), K(t), the standard energy V1 gives V̇1=−q̃̇ᵀDq̃̇+0.5q̃ᵀK̇q̃ when τ_e=0. The authors introduce V2=0.5(q̃̇+αq̃)ᵀH(q̃̇+αq̃)+0.5q̃ᵀ[K+αD−α²H]q̃. Theorem 1 requires an α>0 such that αH−D(t) is negative semidefinite and K̇(t)+αḊ(t)−2αK(t) is negative semidefinite for every t. These are sufficient state-independent profile constraints; strict negative definiteness yields asymptotic stability. A practical eigenvalue-based check selects α from the minimum damping-to-inertia eigenvalue ratio and then validates or modifies the profile. Energy tanks are discussed and simulated only as an alternative comparator: they store dissipated energy and limit stiffness online when the tank lacks energy, whereas the proposed method validates a profile offline and then permits exact execution.
content_summary: The analysis pinpoints the energy source created by stiffness variation and extends the Lyapunov function with a position–velocity cross term so that admissible gain rates can be bounded without using the current robot state. Scalar special cases show that with constant damping, stiffness growth must satisfy k̇<2αk with d>αm; with constant damping ratio, a corresponding stiffness-rate bound is derived. The method is intended to screen impedance trajectories produced by geometry, optimization, learning from demonstration, reinforcement learning, or other generators, not to generate or learn them. Two one-degree-of-freedom simulations compare offline validation against a tank-based online limiter: one reproduces an unstable tracking profile and makes it valid by increasing baseline stiffness, while the other uses a validated regulation profile under temporary force perturbations and shows that the tank modifies stiffness particularly during perturbation. The authors additionally apply the matrix test offline to profiles from three prior works—a KUKA match-lighting experiment, a two-dimensional GMR/minimum-intervention reaching task, and a PI²-learned six-degree-of-freedom via-point task—and report that all pass the sufficient test.
synthesis_role: Provides a formal bridge between fixed impedance and learned or optimized variable impedance: learned gain schedules cannot inherit fixed-gain passivity automatically, so their rates and damping–stiffness relationship must be certified. It contributes an offline sufficient certificate for precomputed profiles while leaving profile acquisition, coupled contact passivity, model uncertainty, and less conservative certification unresolved.
development_link: Compared with classical constant-gain impedance, the paper makes explicit that time-varying stiffness is an active energy port and supplies a matrix condition that can be imposed on precomputed or learned profiles. Compared with online energy-tank stabilization, it trades state dependence and online profile distortion for advance certification and exact profile following, at the cost of exact dynamic decoupling, constant apparent inertia, direct external-effort measurement, and conservatism.

evidence.finding: The classical energy derivative is −q̃̇ᵀDq̃̇+0.5q̃ᵀK̇q̃; a positive stiffness-rate contribution can inject energy whenever position error is nonzero.

evidence.locator: Section III.A, Theorem 1 and Appendix B
evidence.finding: For τ_e=0, constant symmetric positive-definite H, and symmetric positive-definite continuously differentiable K(t), D(t), existence of α>0 satisfying αH−D⪯0 and K̇+αḊ−2αK⪯0 for all time is sufficient for global uniform stability; strict inequalities yield asymptotic stability.
Scalar constant-damping and constant-damping-ratio cases convert the matrix theorem into explicit upper bounds on stiffness growth.

A one-degree-of-freedom sinusoidal tracking profile with mass 10 kg, damping 1 Ns/m, and baseline stiffness 12 is reported unstable; raising baseline stiffness to 18 makes it pass the proposed validation, while the tank method modifies the profile online.

In a validated regulation simulation with temporary constant-force perturbations, the proposed offline-certified controller follows the prescribed stiffness, whereas the tank-based comparator falls back toward constant stiffness when energy is unavailable.

evidence.status: author-reported offline validation of prior data
evidence.finding: The sufficient matrix test reports negative eigenvalues for three previously obtained impedance profiles: match lighting, GMR-based constrained reaching, and PI²-learned via-point motion.

evidence_kind: offline validation of previously collected experimental/learning profiles
boundary_conditions: The theorem is sufficient, not necessary; stable profiles may fail the test, and the authors explicitly call it conservative.

The formal result is for unforced error dynamics τ_e=0. It establishes stability of the nominal variable-impedance system, not input-output passivity or stability with arbitrary active, uncertain, or nonlinear environments.
The desired inertia H must be constant, symmetric, and positive definite; stiffness and damping must be symmetric, positive definite, and continuously differentiable.

Implementation assumes accurate rigid-body dynamics, inverse-dynamics decoupling, and measurement of external effort. The authors state the method does not apply to simplified impedance control with configuration-dependent natural apparent inertia.
Cartesian implementation can violate the constant-H requirement near singular configurations.
Selection of α affects conservatism; a poor α can reject a profile that another valid α would certify.
The comparison with an energy tank is simulation-based and task-dependent; the authors make no general claim that either method is always less conservative.
The three 'real profile' cases are offline tests of data from prior studies, not new hardware trials demonstrating the proposed certificate under novel contact uncertainty.
assumptions: The manipulator obeys the accurately known rigid-body model and inverse dynamics cancels modeled inertia, Coriolis, gravity, and measured external torque as specified.
The reference and gain profiles exist beforehand and are differentiable enough to compute K̇ and Ḋ over the full task.
An α>0 can be found that satisfies both matrix inequalities for every time in the execution interval.
Gain matrices retain symmetry and positive definiteness.
For asymptotic stability, the semidefinite inequalities are strengthened to strict negative definiteness.

reported: Arbitrary impedance variations lose the fixed-gain passivity property and can produce unstable behavior even without contact.
The tank-based alternative is state dependent, cannot guarantee beforehand that the desired profile will be executed, and is sensitive to initial and threshold tank-energy levels.
The proposed certificate is conservative and may reject qualitatively stable impedance profiles.
A poorly chosen α can make the constraints overly conservative.
The constant-inertia requirement needs model knowledge, dynamic decoupling, and external-effort measurement, and is problematic in Cartesian space near singularities.
The method is inapplicable to the simplified controller considered by the authors when apparent inertia equals the configuration-dependent natural robot inertia.
inferred: The theorem does not certify passivity of the time-varying controller at the external interaction port, so stable nominal regulation should not be read as a universal safe-contact guarantee.
Gain schedules learned online or altered unpredictably during execution cannot be certified offline unless their future values and derivatives remain within the theorem's inequalities.
Numerical differentiation and model/sensor error could compromise practical verification or implementation, but robustness margins for these errors are not analyzed.
The offline validation of prior datasets establishes feasibility of the test on selected profiles, not empirical superiority or generality across learned impedance tasks.
